575.title: The Long Discourses, closed
575.hook: from a net that catches every view to a young man bowing in the street
575.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries the Digha Nikaya is studied, and some of its discourses, such as the advice to Sigala, are taught to lay people as a guide for daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your long discourse, and your line, yours. Did you tell someone your scene? Keep it close. Today we close the whole collection and look at the road it took. Day five hundred seventy-five.

The first long discourse begins on a road. The Buddha and his monks are walking between two cities, and behind them walk a wandering teacher and his student, arguing. The teacher criticizes the Buddha the whole way. The student praises him the whole way. Early next morning the monks are buzzing about it, and the Buddha's first words in the whole collection are about that: if people speak against me, or against the teaching, don't get angry. If they praise us, don't get puffed up. Just say what's true and what isn't. Fifty-odd days later, we've reached the end of that road. Today: the Long Discourses, closed.
screen: `TWO TRAVELERS ARGUING BEHIND.` → `NOT ANGRY, NOT PUFFED UP.` → `THE END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of the journey. It starts huge. In that first discourse, the Buddha lays out sixty-two views about the self and the world, and says every such theory is caught among them, like fish in a fine net cast over a small pond. Every one of them, he says, grows out of feeling and craving. It's a teaching about how minds build positions. Then come the kings, the wanderers and the gods, and the long, slow walk of the last journey to the final words. And then, after all that, the collection comes down to earth. A young man named Sigala in the street at dawn, bowing to the directions because his father asked him to. The Buddha doesn't tell him to stop. He tells him what each bow could mean: parents, teachers, spouse, friends, workers, spiritual teachers. Six ways money leaks. How to know a real friend. And after the four kings' protective verses, it closes with Sariputta, counting the teaching aloud so it stays whole. From the net of every view to how you treat the person who cleans your house. That's the long way home: the biggest questions end up at the kitchen table. Tomorrow a new collection begins, much shorter, with poems some scholars count among the oldest Buddhist verses.
screen: `SIXTY-TWO VIEWS CAUGHT IN A NET` · `KINGS, GODS AND THE LAST JOURNEY` · `SIGALA BOWING IN THE STREET` · `FROM EVERY VIEW TO THE KITCHEN TABLE` · then, large: `THE LONG WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall one long discourse from start to finish. Sit and settle. Pick one, perhaps not yesterday's scene: the moonlit king, the last journey, Sigala's six directions, whichever comes. Tell it to yourself in three beats. How it starts. What turns. How it ends. Slowly, as if you were telling a child at bedtime. If a gap appears, don't worry; just notice the gap and go on. Then let the story go quiet and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The Long Discourses. Thirty-four teachings, the Digha Nikaya, running from a net that catches every view to the duties of ordinary life. Today's word.
Your line: the long way home. When a big question fills your head today, bring it home: what would it mean for the next person you'll actually see? Day five hundred seventy-five.

576.title: The oldest poems
576.hook: among the oldest Buddhist verses, first put into English in full in 1881
576.howItsDone: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, especially the discourses on loving-kindness, blessings and the jewel, are among the texts chanted in Theravada temples and homes, and the collection is studied in monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Long Discourses, and your line was the long way home. Did a big question find its way to a real person? Today, a new collection, and a much older sound. Day five hundred seventy-six.

In 1881, in Oxford, a volume came off the press: the tenth book in a series called the Sacred Books of the East. Inside were two Buddhist texts in English, side by side. One was the Dhammapada, translated by Max Muller. The other was a collection of poems, translated from the Pali by a Danish scholar named Viggo Fausboll. Some readers think a few of those poems belong to the oldest layers of the Buddhist canon. Today we open that second book. Today's word: Sutta Nipata.
screen: `OXFORD, 1881.` → `A DANISH SCHOLAR'S TRANSLATION.` → `A SECOND BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: Sutta Nipata means something like the collection of discourses, or the gathering of suttas. It's a small book of short pieces, most of them in verse, sorted into five chapters. Some you may have met: the discourse on loving-kindness, the discourse on blessings, the rhinoceros poem. Others are less familiar. Why do some scholars call parts of it old? They give a few reasons. The language of some verses is archaic, closer to older Indian poetry. The fourth and fifth chapters, called the Chapter of Eights and the Way to the Beyond, are explained line by line by another text inside the canon itself, the Niddesa. To these scholars, a commentary inside the canon suggests the poems were already old and already puzzling while the canon was still being shaped. And the picture of life in them is spare: wanderers, forests, rivers, almost no buildings, very little organization. Some scholars read that as a window onto the earliest days. Others are more cautious and say old verses and newer ones sit side by side. That's why we're reading it slowly. These are poems meant to be said aloud and remembered. You'll hear refrains, lines that come back verse after verse, the way a song comes back to its chorus. Over the next weeks: a snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros, a plowman, a spirit with a threat, and a long list of blessings.
screen: `THE COLLECTION OF DISCOURSES` · `FIVE CHAPTERS, MOSTLY VERSE` · `A COMMENTARY INSIDE THE CANON` · `POEMS MEANT TO BE SAID ALOUD` · then, large: `OLD WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse aloud. Here's one from the other book in that 1881 volume, Max Muller's Dhammapada, a line that calls itself old. Say it with me, slowly, in a normal speaking voice: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love; this is an old rule. Now say it once more on your own, a little slower. Notice the sound in your mouth and the quiet after it. Then sit with the breath and let the line settle. The bell holds the time.
screen: `FOR HATRED DOES NOT CEASE BY HATRED AT ANY TIME.`

segments.voice: Sutta Nipata. The collection of discourses: a small book of short pieces, mostly verse, some of them very old. Today's word.
Your line: old words. Sometime today, say that verse aloud once more, to yourself or to someone else, and let an old sentence be heard again. Day five hundred seventy-six.

577.title: The snake sheds its skin
577.hook: the first poem: letting go as a snake leaves its worn-out skin
577.howItsDone: The Uraga Sutta opens the Sutta Nipata and is studied and chanted in Theravada communities, and Buddhist teachers use its snake-and-skin image when they speak about letting go of anger and pride.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Sutta Nipata, and your line, old words. Did you say a verse aloud? Today, the very first poem in that book, and an animal you might step back from. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

Sometimes, on a hiking trail or under a porch, you find one: a snake's skin, papery, see-through, the whole length of the animal, even the scales over the eyes. Turned inside out, like a sock pulled off in one go. The snake isn't anywhere near. It rubbed its nose on a rough stone, loosened the edge, and crawled forward out of the old self it had outgrown. It didn't tear anything. It just left. The first poem of the Sutta Nipata takes that picture and repeats it, verse after verse, seventeen times. Today: the snake sheds its skin.
screen: `A SKIN ON THE TRAIL.` → `INSIDE OUT, IN ONE PIECE.` → `SEVENTEEN TIMES.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Uraga Sutta. Uraga is a poetic word for snake, the one who moves on its chest. Every verse ends with the same refrain, which runs roughly: such a monk leaves behind this shore and the far shore, as a snake leaves its worn-out old skin. And every verse begins with a different thing let go, each with its own picture. The first: whoever holds back anger as it rises, the way a healer stops snake venom spreading with medicine. Another: whoever cuts off desire completely, like pulling up a lotus that grew in a pond. Another: whoever has broken down pride, the way a great flood sweeps away a flimsy bridge of reeds. And one of the strangest: whoever finds no solid core in any kind of existence, like someone searching fig trees for flowers. Fig trees in that part of the world don't show their flowers; they're hidden inside the fruit. You'll look forever. Notice what the poem keeps saying about the old skin. It's worn out. The snake has already grown past it. Letting go here isn't a heroic tearing. It's leaving what no longer fits. And then the puzzle in the refrain: this shore and the far shore. Elsewhere, the far shore is the goal. Why leave that too? The old commentary offers several readings, one of them simply this world and the next. Some modern readers hear more: the one who's free doesn't cling even to having arrived. The poem doesn't explain itself. It just keeps shedding.
screen: `URAGA: THE ONE WHO MOVES ON ITS CHEST` · `ANGER, DESIRE, PRIDE, LET GO` · `THE SKIN IS ALREADY WORN OUT` · `EVEN THE FAR SHORE?` · then, large: `SHED THE OLD SKIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: shed one old thing. Sit and settle. Ask quietly: what am I still carrying that I've already outgrown? An old grudge. A story about yourself from ten years ago. A habit that made sense once. Don't fight it. Just see that it's worn thin, like papery skin. On the out-breath, picture slipping forward, out of it, and leaving it on the path. You can come back for it later if you really need to. For now, just breathe. The bell holds the time.
The snake sheds its skin. The refrain of the Sutta Nipata's first poem: letting go of anger, desire and pride the way a snake leaves a skin it has already outgrown. Today's word.
screen: `THE SNAKE SHEDS ITS SKIN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: shed the old skin. When that old thing tries to climb back on today, notice it, and step forward out of it again. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

578.title: Rain if you like
578.hook: a herdsman and the Buddha, on the same riverbank, both tell the sky to rain
578.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often retell the Dhaniya poem to talk about two kinds of security, and in Theravada countries the rainy season is also when monks stay in one place for the three-month retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the snake poem, and your line, shed the old skin. Did the old thing try to climb back on? Today, a storm is coming, and two men answer it in verse. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

The weather app says heavy rain tonight. And there's a particular feeling, if you're lucky enough to have it: groceries in, laundry dry, windows shut, someone you love on the couch. Let it pour. The second poem of the Sutta Nipata starts right there. A cattle herder named Dhaniya, on the bank of the Mahi river, with the monsoon clouds rolling in. He's done everything right, and he's proud of it, and he sings it to the sky. Today: rain if you like.
screen: `HEAVY RAIN TONIGHT.` → `DHANIYA ON THE RIVERBANK.` → `HE SINGS TO THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Dhaniya's verse goes something like this. My rice is cooked, my cows are milked. I live with my people by the river. My hut is roofed, my fire is lit. So rain if you like, sky. And from nearby, another voice answers in the same rhythm. It's the Buddha, who happens to be spending one night on the same riverbank. I'm free of anger, my stubbornness is gone. I stay one night by the river. My hut is open, my fire is out. So rain if you like, sky. Hear the play on words? Dhaniya's fire is the cooking fire. The Buddha's fire is the fire of craving, and it's gone out. Dhaniya's roof keeps the rain away. The Buddha's hut is open, nothing to protect. They trade verses. Dhaniya: my cattle are strong, my wife is faithful, my sons are healthy. The Buddha: my raft is built, I've crossed the flood, I'm nobody's servant. Then the sky opens. A great rain falls, and Dhaniya and his wife, the poem says, go for refuge and ask to go forth. Only then does Mara join in: whoever has children delights in children; whoever has cattle delights in cattle. And the Buddha answers him: whoever has children grieves over children; whoever has cattle grieves over cattle. The poem sets the two verses side by side. What we have makes us glad and makes us worry, often in the same breath. And the poem never mocks Dhaniya. His security is real. It just shows a second kind of shelter beside it.
screen: `MY RICE IS COOKED, MY HUT IS ROOFED` · `MY HUT IS OPEN, MY FIRE IS OUT` · `THE RAIN FALLS` · `GLAD OVER IT, GRIEVING OVER IT` · then, large: `RAIN IF YOU LIKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel what you already have. Sit and settle. Name, like Dhaniya, three shelters you have right now: a roof, a meal, a person. Let yourself be glad of them. Then, gently, notice the worry that sits right next to each one. You don't have to fix it. Just see both: the gladness and the worry, holding hands. Then let them both rest, and listen to the breath as if it were rain on a roof. The bell holds the time.
Rain if you like. The refrain of the Dhaniya poem: a herdsman safe in his hut, and the Buddha free with an open one, both saying it to the same sky. Today's word.
Your line: rain if you like. When something unwelcome rolls in today, a delay, a mood, actual rain, try saying it under your breath. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

579.title: The rhinoceros horn
579.hook: a poem whose every verse ends: wander alone like the rhinoceros horn
579.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners sometimes take periods of solitary retreat, and Theravada teachers draw on the rhinoceros poem's refrain, eko care khaggavisanakappo, when they speak about solitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dhaniya and the Buddha on the riverbank, and your line, rain if you like. Did you say it to something unwelcome? Today, an animal that walks by itself. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

The Indian rhinoceros has one horn. One. And it mostly keeps to itself, grazing through tall grass by the rivers, a huge animal that doesn't travel in a herd. In the British Library there's a birch-bark scroll, written in a language called Gandhari, which its editor dates to around the first century. It's among the oldest Buddhist manuscripts known, and one of the texts on it is a poem about that animal. Today: the rhinoceros horn.
screen: `ONE HORN.` → `A BIRCH-BARK SCROLL.` → `A VERY OLD MANUSCRIPT.`

segments.voice: The poem is the third in the Sutta Nipata, the Khaggavisana Sutta, a long run of verses. Verse after verse ends with the same refrain in Pali: eko care khaggavisanakappo. Wander alone, like the rhinoceros horn. Visana is a horn, and khaggavisana names the rhinoceros horn. One horn, standing alone on the animal's head, and one walker, standing alone in the world. Some translators say like the rhinoceros, some say like its horn; the image works either way. Listen to what the verses ask you to set down. Laying aside violence toward every living being, wishing harm to none. Not wishing even for a son, let alone a companion. Seeing that closeness breeds attachment, and attachment breeds sorrow. Like a deer in the forest, unbound, going wherever it wants to graze. Like a lion not startled by sounds, like the wind not caught in a net, like a lotus not stained by water. Is this lonely? The poem doesn't sound lonely. It sounds free. The old commentary says these verses were spoken by solitary buddhas, people who woke up on their own and lived without a community. That's the tradition's reading; the poem itself just keeps returning to the one horn. And it isn't the whole story. Early in the poem, a few verses turn a corner, and we'll hear those tomorrow. For today, stay with the rhinoceros: steady, unhurried, not needing anyone's permission to walk through the grass.
screen: `ONE HORN, ONE WALKER` · `SET DOWN VIOLENCE AND CLINGING` · `A DEER, A LION, THE WIND, A LOTUS` · `FREE, NOT LONELY` · then, large: `ALONE LIKE THE RHINOCEROS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one solo walk, and begin it now in the body. Sit and settle. Feel your own weight, the way the rhinoceros feels the ground. Nobody needs to approve this breath. Nobody is watching it. Just you, breathing, steady. Then decide when today you'll take a short walk alone, no phone in your hand, no podcast. Five or ten minutes. You'll walk the way the poem walks: not running from anyone, not looking for anyone. The bell holds the time.
The rhinoceros horn. The refrain of the Sutta Nipata's third poem: wander alone, like the one horn of the Indian rhinoceros, steady and free. Today's word.
Your line: alone like the rhinoceros. Take your solo walk today, and notice what you hear when no one is talking to you. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

580.title: Or with a friend
580.hook: in the middle of the rhinoceros poem, a door opens: if you find a wise companion, walk with them
580.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching speaks of the kalyanamitta, the good or noble friend, and Buddhists practice in groups, with a teacher, or with a trusted companion, alongside times of solitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the one-horned rhinoceros, and your line, alone like the rhinoceros. Did you take your solo walk? What did you hear? Today, the same poem turns a corner. Day five hundred eighty.

Verse after verse, the rhinoceros poem ends the same way: wander alone. Read it fast and you'd think the poem's whole message is: don't need anyone. But look closely near the start. Two verses sit there, side by side, and they don't end the way the others do. They start with the word if. If you find someone. It's like reading a long letter from a friend who keeps saying I'm fine on my own, I'm fine on my own, and then, partway down the page, writes: unless you'd like to come. Today: or with a friend.
screen: `VERSE AFTER VERSE: WANDER ALONE.` → `THEN, EARLY ON: IF.` → `UNLESS YOU'D LIKE TO COME.`

segments.voice: Here's what the verse says, roughly. If you find a wise companion, a fellow traveler who lives well and is steady, then walk with them, overcoming every danger, glad and mindful. And the next verse: if you don't find one like that, then walk alone, like a king who has left a conquered kingdom behind, like an elephant alone in the forest. So the solitude was never the goal. It's what you do when the right companion isn't there. The poem even names what makes a companion right. Wise, the Pali word is nipaka, meaning skilled, discerning. Living well. Steady. Someone who makes the dangers smaller, not bigger. And a little later comes a line that sounds almost like a proverb: we praise the blessing of companionship. Keep company with those better than you or equal to you. If you can't find them, live blamelessly and walk alone. Elsewhere in the discourses, an exchange fits right here. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, says: good friendship is half of the spiritual life. And the Buddha corrects him: don't say that, Ananda. Good friendship is the whole of the spiritual life. So the tradition holds both: the one horn and the good friend. Not a contradiction. Two pictures of the same freedom. You don't need a crowd. And when someone wise and kind turns up on your road, you don't need to walk alone either.
screen: `IF YOU FIND A WISE COMPANION` · `IF NOT, WALK ALONE` · `WISE, STEADY, LIVING WELL` · `FRIENDSHIP IS THE WHOLE OF IT` · then, large: `OR WITH A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring a good friend to mind. Sit and settle. Think of someone who makes the road safer: wise, steady, kind. Maybe they're near, maybe far, maybe they've died. Picture walking beside them, not talking much, matching steps. Feel what their company does to your breathing. If there's no one like that right now, picture the friend you'd like to find, and the friend you'd like to be. Then rest in that companionship. The bell holds the time.
Or with a friend. The turn in the rhinoceros poem: if you find a wise and steady companion, walk with them, glad and mindful. Today's word.
Your line: or with a friend. Ask one good friend to walk with you this week, even ten minutes, even on a call while you both walk. Day five hundred eighty.

581.title: Faith the seed
581.hook: a brahmin farmer with five hundred plows tells the Buddha to plow for his food
581.howItsDone: Theravada monastics live on alms and do not farm or handle money; lay supporters offer food, and the Kasibharadvaja poem is one text teachers use to explain how monastic and lay life support each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the turn in the rhinoceros poem, and your line, or with a friend. Did you ask someone to walk with you? Today ends the week, out in a field at sowing time. Day five hundred eighty-one.

Sowing day on a big farm in Magadha. A brahmin named Kasi Bharadvaja has five hundred plows out in his fields, and at lunchtime he's handing out food to the workers. Then a man with a bowl walks up and stands quietly at the edge of the line. The farmer looks him over, and he isn't impressed. I plow and I sow, he says, and then I eat. You should plow and sow too, and then you can eat. It's a fair point, the kind people still make about anyone whose work you can't see. The Buddha's answer is today's poem. Today: faith the seed.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED PLOWS AT SOWING TIME.` → `I PLOW, THEN I EAT.` → `YOU SHOULD TOO.`

segments.voice: The Buddha says: I plow and sow too, brahmin, and then I eat. The farmer is puzzled. We don't see your yoke, your plow, your oxen. So the Buddha describes his farm, in verse. Faith is the seed. Discipline is the rain. Wisdom is my yoke and plow. Conscience is the pole, the mind the strap, mindfulness my plowshare and goad. Guarded in body and speech, moderate in food. Truth is how I weed. Effort is my ox, pulling toward freedom without turning back. And this plowing, he says, has the deathless as its harvest. Notice where faith sits. It's the seed, the very first thing, small, put into the ground before anything shows. Saddha, the Pali word, can be translated faith, trust or confidence. In this poem it isn't the harvest. It's the trust that gets you to begin, the way you plant a seed you can't yet see growing. Then wisdom and effort and mindfulness have to do the work. The farmer is moved and offers milk-rice in a bronze bowl. And the Buddha declines it: food given in payment for verses, he says, isn't for him. In the end the farmer asks to go forth. That's this week, too. A whole collection closed. The oldest poems opened. A snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros alone, a friend on the road, and now a field. Each one sets an ordinary picture, a skin, a roof, a horn, a road, a plow, beside a deeper one.
screen: `I PLOW AND SOW TOO` · `FAITH THE SEED, WISDOM THE PLOW` · `TRUST THAT GETS YOU TO BEGIN` · `A WEEK OF ORDINARY PICTURES` · then, large: `FAITH THE SEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your plow. Sit and settle. In the poem, each tool has a job. Ask: what's my seed, the small trust that got me started on something good? What's my plow, the steady tool I use? Patience, honesty, an early alarm, a notebook. And what's my ox, the effort that keeps pulling? Name each one quietly. Then rest, and let the breath be the slow work of a field: nothing to force, just showing up. The bell holds the time.
Faith the seed. The Buddha's farming poem: trust is the seed you plant first, then wisdom plows, effort pulls, and the harvest is freedom. Today's word.
Your line: faith the seed. Plant one small seed today: begin one good thing you can't yet see the end of. Day five hundred eighty-one.

original.note: Pali saddha: faith, trust, confidence. in Sn 1.4, the seed.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means believing without evidence.
what it means: in this poem faith is the seed, the trust that gets you to begin, with wisdom and effort doing the work after.
what a scholar hears: saddha is also rendered confidence; some early texts link it to a teacher one has tested, and the Kasibharadvaja Sutta appears in both the Sutta Nipata and the Samyutta Nikaya.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.4, Kasibharadvaja Sutta (also Samyutta Nikaya 7.11)
